tagline: Cross-tipped churches mark a farming region shaped by generations of Catholic building.
intro: The Land of the Cross-Tipped Churches Scenic Byway runs through western Ohio farm country, where large Catholic churches dominate the architecture. Ohio’s Department of Transportation describes the 38-mile route through its cross-tipped churches on the National Register of Historic Places. The towers can be seen from far away, giving the region its name.

Under missionary priest Francis de Sales Brunner, the Society of the Most Precious Blood founded churches, schools and seminaries across the region. The first generation of buildings was largely wooden or simple brick. Later construction replaced most of them; Anton DeCurtins and his descendants built many of the large Gothic Revival churches in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Padua, also known locally as St. Anthony, stands at SR 49 and St. Anthony Road. To the south, Fort Recovery brings SR 49 and SR 119 together. Farther east, SR 119 connects St. Henry, Maria Stein and Minster. McCartyville lies at SR 29 and SR 119 on the region’s eastern edge, where Sacred Heart’s 1911 rectory is a listed historic building.

moments.title: St. Henry
moments.text: St. Henry’s congregation outgrew successive church buildings. A small frame building went up in 1840, followed by a brick church completed in 1854. Construction of the present church began in 1895 and finished in 1897, with parishioners doing much of the work. Adolphus Druiding designed it, and the DeCurtins Brothers were the contractors. The Gothic Revival building has a Latin-cross plan and a central belfry and clock tower approximately 200 feet tall. It remains home to an active congregation. Its rose windows and brick walls belong to the region’s generation of Gothic churches with a single central tower.

moments.title: Maria Stein
moments.text: Maria Stein grew from two communities drawn together by a railroad. St. Johns, established in 1833, stood east of the settlement the Cincinnati, Hamilton, and Dayton Railway chose for its route. Businesses shifted toward the tracks, and the communities merged as Maria Stein. The community is home to the Shrine of the Holy Relics, whose first collection was assembled by Father Francis de Sales Brunner. A separate relic chapel was established in 1892, where the Sisters of the Precious Blood conducted a continuous vigil. St. John the Baptist Catholic Church, built in 1889, was destroyed by fire on May 29, 2025.

moments.title: Minster
moments.text: St. Augustine’s twin spires are younger than the church beneath them. The building dates to 1848; Anton Goehr’s Gothic spires were added in 1874. St. Augustine served as one of three mother churches for the Society of the Precious Blood from the middle of the nineteenth century until its end. It is the only one of those three remaining. The village itself began as Stallostown in 1832 and took the name Minster in 1836, after the Münster region of Westphalia from which many settlers came. The church stands on North Hanover Street and continues in use as a parish church.
moments.notice: St. Augustine’s paired Gothic spires were added to its earlier church building.
